steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our survey on large language model security and privacy. Explain what LLMs are and why they matter, why the security community cares, pose our research questions, summarize the good / bad / ugly categories we found, and list our contributions and the paper organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. What an LLM is and what a capable one should do
2. Popular LLMs of 2023 and their applications
3. LLMs in the security community: early results
4. Research questions
5. Literature review and the good / bad / ugly categories
6. Contributions
7. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLM definition
- language model with massive parameters, pretraining tasks (masked language modeling, autoregressive prediction)
- models contextualized text semantics and probabilities from large amounts of text
- four key features of a capable LLM: (i) comprehension of natural language context, (ii) human-like text generation, (iii) contextual awareness esp. knowledge-intensive domains, (iv) strong instruction-following -> problem-solving, decision-making

2. LLMs in 2023
- many developed/released in 2023, very popular
- ChatGPT (OpenAI), LLaMA (Meta AI), Dolly 2.0 (Databricks)
- ChatGPT: over 180 million users
- language-related applications: search engines, customer support, translation
- general scenarios: code generation, healthcare, finance, education
- adaptability across industries

3. Security community
- Feb 2023 study: GPT-3 found 213 vulnerabilities in a code repository, only 4 false positives
- leading commercial tool found only 99
- LLM security papers at top conferences
- IEEE S&P 2023: Hammond Pearce et al., commercial LLMs on synthetic, hand-crafted, real-world security bugs; solved all synthetic + hand-crafted
- NDSS 2024: Fuzz4All, LLMs for input generation/mutation, autoprompting, fuzzing loop

4. RQs
- RQ1: positive impact on security & privacy, advantages for security community
- RQ2: risks and threats from using LLMs in cybersecurity
- RQ3: vulnerabilities/weaknesses in LLMs, how to defend

5. Review: 281 papers, three groups
- The Good (§ 4): most papers; code security (whole code life cycle: secure coding, test case generation, vulnerable/malicious code detection, code fixing); data security & privacy (integrity, confidentiality, reliability, traceability); mostly outperform traditional approaches
- The Bad (§ 5): five attack groups: hardware-level (side-channel), OS-level, software-level (malware), network-level (phishing), user-level (misinformation, social engineering, scientific misconduct); user-level most prevalent, 32 papers, human-like reasoning; no direct OS/hardware access yet, threat could escalate
- The Ugly (§ 6): AI model inherent vulnerabilities (data poisoning, backdoor, training data extraction) vs non-AI model inherent (remote code execution, prompt injection, side channels); defenses: architecture, training (corpora cleaning, optimization), inference (instruction pre-processing, malicious detection, generation post-processing); gaps: model/parameter extraction mostly theoretical, scale + confidentiality, output censorship blocks black-box ML attacks, little work on architecture and safety (compute cost), safe instruction tuning needs work

6. Contributions
- first to summarize role of LLMs in security and privacy, covering all three aspects; other surveys cover one or two
- findings: more positive than negative; LLMs beat SOTA for securing code/data; user-level attacks most prevalent

7. Organization: § 2 background, § 3 overview, § 4 good, § 5 bad, § 6 threats/vulnerabilities/countermeasures, § 7 other topics and directions, § 9 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A large language model is a language model that has massive parameters and goes through pretraining tasks (e.g., masked language modeling and autoregressive prediction) so that it can understand and process human language. It does this by modeling the contextualized text semantics and probabilities from large amounts of text data. A capable LLM should have four key features: (i) it deeply comprehends natural language context; (ii) it can generate human-like text; (iii) it has contextual awareness, especially in knowledge-intensive domains; (iv) it follows instructions well, which is useful for problem-solving and decision-making.

A number of LLMs were developed and released in 2023 and they became very popular. Some notable examples are OpenAI's ChatGPT, Meta AI's LLaMA, and Databricks' Dolly 2.0. ChatGPT alone has a user base of over 180 million. LLMs now have many different applications in many domains. They provide technical support to domains that are directly related to language processing (e.g., search engines, customer support, translation) and they are also used in more general scenarios such as code generation, healthcare, finance, and education. This shows that they are adaptable and can streamline language-related tasks in a lot of different industries and contexts.

LLMs are also getting popular in the security community. As of February 2023, a research study reported that GPT-3 found 213 security vulnerabilities in a code repository, and only 4 of them were false positives. One of the leading commercial tools on the market only found 99 vulnerabilities. Recently there have also been several LLM-powered security papers in prestigious conferences. For instance, in IEEE S&P 2023, Hammond Pearce et al. did a comprehensive investigation using various commercially available LLMs, and evaluated them on synthetic, hand-crafted, and real-world security bug scenarios. The results were promising, because the LLMs solved all of the synthetic and hand-crafted scenarios. In NDSS 2024, a tool called Fuzz4All showed how LLMs can be used for input generation and mutation, together with a new autoprompting technique and fuzzing loop.

These first attempts lead us to three important security-related research questions:

- • RQ1. How do LLMs have a positive impact on security and privacy in different domains, and what advantages do they give the security community?

- • RQ2. What potential risks and threats come from using LLMs in cybersecurity?

- • RQ3. What vulnerabilities and weaknesses do LLMs have, and how can we defend against those threats?

- literature review: 281 papers on LLMs + security and privacy, three groups (good / bad / ugly)
- The Good (§ 4): most papers; code security over whole code life cycle (secure coding, test case generation, vulnerable/malicious code detection, code fixing); data security & privacy (integrity, confidentiality, reliability, traceability); LLM-based methods mostly beat traditional ones
- The Bad (§ 5): five attack groups (hardware, OS, software, network, user level); user-level most common (32 papers) due to human-like reasoning; threaten security and privacy; no OS/hardware access yet, could escalate
- The Ugly (§ 6): AI model inherent vs non-AI model inherent vulnerabilities; defenses in architecture, training (corpora cleaning, optimization), inference (instruction pre-processing, malicious detection, generation post-processing); open gaps: model/parameter extraction mostly theoretical, scale + confidentiality, output censorship, architecture vs safety, safe instruction tuning
- Contributions: first survey covering all three aspects; findings: more positive than negative, LLMs beat SOTA for code/data security, user-level attacks most common
- Organization: § 2 to § 7, conclusion § 9

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A large language model is a language model that has massive parameters and goes through pretraining tasks (e.g., masked language modeling and autoregressive prediction) so that it can understand and process human language. It does this by modeling the contextualized text semantics and probabilities from large amounts of text data. A capable LLM should have four key features: (i) it deeply comprehends natural language context; (ii) it can generate human-like text; (iii) it has contextual awareness, especially in knowledge-intensive domains; (iv) it follows instructions well, which is useful for problem-solving and decision-making.

A number of LLMs were developed and released in 2023 and they became very popular. Some notable examples are OpenAI's ChatGPT, Meta AI's LLaMA, and Databricks' Dolly 2.0. ChatGPT alone has a user base of over 180 million. LLMs now have many different applications in many domains. They provide technical support to domains that are directly related to language processing (e.g., search engines, customer support, translation) and they are also used in more general scenarios such as code generation, healthcare, finance, and education. This shows that they are adaptable and can streamline language-related tasks in a lot of different industries and contexts.

LLMs are also getting popular in the security community. As of February 2023, a research study reported that GPT-3 found 213 security vulnerabilities in a code repository, and only 4 of them were false positives. One of the leading commercial tools on the market only found 99 vulnerabilities. Recently there have also been several LLM-powered security papers in prestigious conferences. For instance, in IEEE S&P 2023, Hammond Pearce et al. did a comprehensive investigation using various commercially available LLMs, and evaluated them on synthetic, hand-crafted, and real-world security bug scenarios. The results were promising, because the LLMs solved all of the synthetic and hand-crafted scenarios. In NDSS 2024, a tool called Fuzz4All showed how LLMs can be used for input generation and mutation, together with a new autoprompting technique and fuzzing loop.

These first attempts lead us to three important security-related research questions:

- • RQ1. How do LLMs have a positive impact on security and privacy in different domains, and what advantages do they give the security community?

- • RQ2. What potential risks and threats come from using LLMs in cybersecurity?

- • RQ3. What vulnerabilities and weaknesses do LLMs have, and how can we defend against those threats?

To answer these questions, we did a careful literature review and collected 281 papers about the intersection of LLMs with security and privacy. We put these papers into three groups: papers about applications that are good for security (i.e., the good), papers about applications that could have a bad impact on security (i.e., the bad), and papers that discuss security vulnerabilities in LLMs together with possible defenses (i.e., the ugly). In more detail:

- • The Good (§ 4): Mostly, LLMs have a positive impact on the security community, since the largest number of papers are about improving security. LLMs have contributed both to code security and to data security and privacy. For code security, LLMs have been used for the whole life cycle of the code (e.g., secure coding, test case generation, vulnerable code detection, malicious code detection, and code fixing). For data security and privacy, LLMs have been used to ensure data integrity, data confidentiality, data reliability, and data traceability. Also, most researchers found that LLM-based methods do better than traditional approaches when compared to state-of-the-art methods.

- • The Bad (§ 5): LLMs also have offensive applications against security and privacy. We put the attacks into five groups: hardware-level attacks (e.g., side-channel attacks), OS-level attacks (e.g., analyzing information from operating systems), software-level attacks (e.g., creating malware), network-level attacks (e.g., network phishing), and user-level attacks (e.g., misinformation, social engineering, scientific misconduct). User-level attacks are the most common, with 32 papers, because LLMs have human-like reasoning abilities. These attacks are a threat to both security (e.g., malware attacks) and privacy (e.g., social engineering). Right now LLMs do not have direct access to OS and hardware-level functions. If they get that access, the potential threats of LLMs could become worse.

- • The Ugly (§ 6): We look at the vulnerabilities and defenses in LLMs. We divide vulnerabilities into two main groups: AI Model Inherent Vulnerabilities (e.g., data poisoning, backdoor attacks, training data extraction) and Non-AI Model Inherent Vulnerabilities (e.g., remote code execution, prompt injection, side channels). These attacks are a threat in two ways, to security (e.g., remote code execution attacks) and to privacy (e.g., data extraction). Defenses for LLMs are divided into strategies in the architecture and strategies applied in the training and inference phases. Training phase defenses include corpora cleaning and optimization methods, and inference phase defenses include instruction pre-processing, malicious detection, and generation post-processing. Together these defenses try to improve the security, robustness, and ethical alignment of LLMs. We found that model extraction, parameter extraction, and similar attacks have not had much research attention and are still mostly theoretical with little practical exploration. Because LLMs have such a huge number of parameters, traditional approaches work less well, and powerful LLMs are kept confidential, which also protects them from conventional attacks. Strict censorship of LLM outputs makes even black-box ML attacks hard. Also, there is very little research on how model architecture affects LLM safety, partly because of high computational costs. Safe instruction tuning is a recent development and needs more investigation.

Our work makes two contributions. First, we are the first to summarize the role of LLMs in security and privacy. We look in depth at the positive impacts of LLMs on security, their potential risks and threats, the vulnerabilities in LLMs, and the defense mechanisms against them. Other surveys may only focus on one or two aspects, like beneficial applications, offensive applications, vulnerabilities, or defenses. As far as we know, our survey is the first one that covers all three key aspects related to security and privacy. Second, we made several interesting discoveries. For example, our research shows that LLMs contribute more positively than negatively to security and privacy. We also see that most researchers agree that LLMs do better than state-of-the-art methods when they are used to secure code or data. At the same time, user-level attacks are clearly the most common, mostly because of the human-like reasoning abilities of LLMs.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. § 2 gives a brief introduction to LLMs. § 3 presents the overview of our work. § 4 explores the good impacts of using LLMs. § 5 discusses the negative impacts on security and privacy. § 6 discusses the common threats and vulnerabilities of LLMs and the countermeasures to reduce these risks. § 7 discusses LLMs in other security related topics and possible directions. § 9 concludes the paper.

This shows their adaptability and their potential to streamline language-related tasks across diverse industries and contexts.

LLMs are gaining popularity within the security community. As of February 2023, a research study reported that GPT-3 uncovered 213 security vulnerabilities (only 4 of which were false positives) [15] in a code repository, whereas one of the leading commercial tools on the market detected only 99 vulnerabilities. More recently, several LLM-powered security papers have appeared in prestigious conferences. For instance, in IEEE S&P 2023, Hammond Pearce et al. [16] conducted a comprehensive investigation of various commercially available LLMs, evaluating them across synthetic, hand-crafted, and real-world security bug scenarios. The results are promising: the LLMs successfully addressed all synthetic and hand-crafted scenarios. In NDSS 2024, a tool named Fuzz4All [17] demonstrated the use of LLMs for input generation and mutation, along with a new autoprompting technique and fuzzing loop.

These initial attempts lead us to three crucial security-related research questions:

- • RQ1. How do LLMs make a positive impact on security and privacy across diverse domains, and what advantages do they offer to the security community?

- • RQ2. What potential risks and threats emerge from the use of LLMs within cybersecurity?

- • RQ3. What vulnerabilities and weaknesses exist within LLMs, and how can we defend against those threats?

To address these questions comprehensively, we conducted a careful literature review and collected 281 papers on the intersection of LLMs with security and privacy. We categorized these papers into three groups: those highlighting security-beneficial applications (i.e., the good), those exploring applications that could have adverse impacts on security (i.e., the bad), and those discussing security vulnerabilities (along with potential defense mechanisms) within LLMs (i.e., the ugly). More specifically:

- • The Good (§ 4): LLMs have a predominantly positive impact on the security community, as shown by the largest number of papers being dedicated to enhancing security. LLMs have contributed to both code security and data security and privacy. In code security, LLMs have been used across the whole life cycle of the code (e.g., secure coding, test case generation, vulnerable code detection, malicious code detection, and code fixing). In data security and privacy, LLMs have been applied to ensure data integrity, data confidentiality, data reliability, and data traceability. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, most researchers found that LLM-based methods outperform traditional approaches.

- • The Bad (§ 5): LLMs also have offensive applications against security and privacy. We categorized the attacks into five groups: hardware-level attacks (e.g., side-channel attacks), OS-level attacks (e.g., analyzing information from operating systems), software-level attacks (e.g., creating malware), network-level attacks (e.g., network phishing), and user-level attacks (e.g., misinformation, social engineering, scientific misconduct). User-level attacks, with 32 papers, are the most prevalent because of LLMs' human-like reasoning abilities. These attacks threaten both security (e.g., malware attacks) and privacy (e.g., social engineering). Currently, LLMs lack direct access to OS and hardware-level functions; the potential threats of LLMs could escalate if they gain such access.

- • The Ugly (§ 6): We explore the vulnerabilities and defenses in LLMs, categorizing vulnerabilities into two main groups: AI Model Inherent Vulnerabilities (e.g., data poisoning, backdoor attacks, training data extraction) and Non-AI Model Inherent Vulnerabilities (e.g., remote code execution, prompt injection, side channels). These attacks pose a dual threat, involving both security concerns (e.g., remote code execution attacks) and privacy issues (e.g., data extraction). Defenses for LLMs are divided into strategies placed in the architecture and those applied during the training and inference phases. Training phase defenses involve corpora cleaning and optimization methods, while inference phase defenses include instruction pre-processing, malicious detection, and generation post-processing. Together, these defenses aim to enhance the security, robustness, and ethical alignment of LLMs. We found that model extraction, parameter extraction, and similar attacks have received limited research attention and remain primarily theoretical, with little practical exploration. The vast scale of LLM parameters makes traditional approaches less effective, and the confidentiality of powerful LLMs further shields them from conventional attacks. Strict censorship of LLM outputs challenges even black-box ML attacks. Meanwhile, research on the impact of model architecture on LLM safety is scarce, partly due to high computational costs. Safe instruction tuning, a recent development, requires further investigation.

Our work makes a dual contribution. First, we are the first to summarize the role of LLMs in security and privacy. We look deeply into the positive impacts of LLMs on security, their potential risks and threats, vulnerabilities in LLMs, and the corresponding defense mechanisms. Other surveys may focus on one or two specific aspects, such as beneficial applications, offensive applications, vulnerabilities, or defenses. To the best of our knowledge, our survey is the first to cover all three key aspects related to security and privacy. Second, we have made several interesting discoveries. For instance, our research reveals that LLMs contribute more positively than negatively to security and privacy. Moreover, we observe that most researchers agree that LLMs outperform state-of-the-art methods when used for securing code or data. At the same time, it is evident that user-level attacks are the most prevalent, largely because of the human-like reasoning abilities of LLMs.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We begin with a brief introduction to LLMs in § 2. § 3 presents the overview of our work. In § 4, we explore the beneficial impacts of employing LLMs. § 5 discusses the negative impacts on security and privacy. In § 6, we discuss the prevalent threats and vulnerabilities associated with LLMs, as well as countermeasures to mitigate these risks. § 7 discusses LLMs in other security related topics and possible directions. We conclude the paper in § 9.
